definition: A development guideline advising against implementing functionality until it is actually needed by concrete requirements.
ruleOfThumb: Implement the simplest thing that could possibly work for current requirements; defer extensibility until it is required.

questions.prompt: A team adds an elaborate permissions engine before any roles or complexity exist. What best describes that decision?

options.text: They implemented functionality before it was necessary based on speculative future requirements rather than current business needs.
options.explanation: This is implementing for hypothetical future needs rather than present requirements. That creates needless complexity and maintenance burden when the functionality may never be required.

options.text: They made a defensive design choice that responsibly anticipates foreseeable changes and reduces future integration costs.
options.explanation: While anticipating change can sometimes be appropriate, in this scenario there is no evidence of imminent need so the complexity is premature and costly.

options.text: They duplicated existing logic into a separate module to increase modularity and promote decoupled responsibilities.
options.explanation: Duplicating logic into a new module can be a refactor for clarity, but the core issue here is adding unused capability rather than improving present modularity.

options.text: They followed a compliance driven requirement to add audit hooks now for upcoming regulatory deadlines.
options.explanation: If compliance drove the change it would be justified, but the scenario states there is no current need, so regulatory justification is not present and complexity is premature.

questions.prompt: Review the code change below. What is the primary problem introduced by this change?

options.text: The change introduces premature abstraction coupling the module to hypothetical analytics that are not yet required by product behavior.
options.explanation: Adding hooks and optional dependencies for analytics before a concrete need introduces coupling and test surface area without delivering current value.

options.text: The change creates hidden operational cost and testing burden by adding an unused external dependency interface now.
options.explanation: This is a real concern, but it describes a symptom of premature abstraction; the root problem is the speculative addition rather than just operational cost.

options.text: The change improves forward compatibility by preparing pluggable hooks to avoid larger future refactors across services.
options.explanation: Preparing pluggable hooks can help future changes, but without a current requirement it risks wasted effort and complicates the current codebase unnecessarily.

options.text: The change addresses a compliance requirement by adding auditing stubs to capture events for future reporting needs.
options.explanation: If compliance required these hooks then they would be warranted; in the given snippet the comments indicate speculation rather than a compliance driver, making the change premature.

questions.prompt: Two implementations were proposed. Which version aligns better with current needs and why?

options.text: Version A prevents future refactors by implementing an extensible plugin architecture at implementation time.
options.explanation: Although extensibility can reduce some future refactors, introducing a plugin pipeline now adds complexity and maintenance cost for a capability that may never be needed. The simpler implementation better serves current requirements and keeps options open for refactoring when real need appears.

options.text: Version B provides the minimal, required implementation without speculative extensibility and lower immediate complexity.
options.explanation: Version B follows the principle of implementing the simplest thing that works for current requirements. It minimizes code surface, test burden, and cognitive load. If extensibility becomes necessary later, a targeted refactor to introduce a plugin system will be cheaper and informed by real requirements rather than speculation. See Pragmatic Programmer and XP guidance on avoiding premature generality.
